newsitem.title: USA: Va. convict awaits fate after jurors seek clemency.
newsitem.headline: Va. convict awaits fate after jurors seek clemency.

text.p: Death row inmate Joseph Patrick Payne awaited word on Thursday on whether his life would be spared after four members of the jury that convicted him of murder, and the victim's mother, said they believed he was innocent.
Payne was scheduled to die via lethal injection at 9 p.m. EST (0200 GMT) on Thursday for the 1985 slaying of fellow inmate David Wayne Dunford, unless Virginia Gov. George Allen granted him clemency.
A spokesman for Allen said the governor was considering the clemency petition and planned to make a statement sometime on Thursday.
Allen, a conservative Republican who won office by promising to get tough on crime, has allowed 10 executions to proceed since he took office in 1994.
On Thursday the U.S. Supreme Court voted 7-2 to deny his request for a stay of execution. The high court said only that Justices John Paul Stevens and Ruth Bader Ginsburg would grant the application.

Payne was convicted and sentenced to die for the March 3, 1985, slaying of Dunford, 28, who was serving a 15-year sentence for auto theft at the Powhatan Correctional Centre near Richmond. Dunford was set on fire in his cell and died nine days later without identifying his killer.

At the time Payne was serving a life sentence at Powhatan for the 1981 capital murder of grocery store owner Louise Winslow in Bristow, Virginia. He shot Winslow during a robbery as his three-year-old son sat outside in the escape vehicle.

In an affidavit signed Oct. 29 and sent to the governor as part of Payne's clemency petition, Dunford's mother, Reba Dunford, said, "I have doubts that Joe Payne killed my son. I can think of no greater tragedy than killing an innocent man. Please do not let this happen, Gov. Allen. It would be a terrible mistake and one that I could not live with."

Witnesses at Payne's trial were prison inmates, and the key testimony came from inmate Robert Francis "Dirty Smitty" Smith. Smith was the only man who claimed to have witnessed Dunford's slaying and he fingered Payne as the killer.
But another inmate testified that he saw Payne in the shower at the time that Dunford was set on fire.

The jury accepted Smith's testimony, and did not learn that he later recanted his testimony and then changed his story again, nor did they hear that other inmates had come forward after the trial to say Payne was innocent.

"We did not believe much of what any of those guys said," said juror Phyllis Joan Forrester in an affidavit after learning of the new evidence. "Our decision to find him guilty of this crime was based on more of a gut feeling we all shared that he was guilty."

"I can't begin to say how heavily this has weighed on me," said juror Shelly Brydie Gray in an affidavit. "I have often thought that this mistake would be something I would have to one day settle with God."
"I think it's fair to say it's pretty unprecedented," said Stephen Bright, director of the Southern Centre for Human Rights in Atlanta and an expert in capital punishment, of the Payne case.

Payne, who planned to spend Thursday visiting with his wife, some Catholic priests and his lawyer, would be the 33rd inmate to be put to death in Virginia since the 1977 resumption of the death penalty. Only Texas and Florida have executed more prisoners.
